i kept watching solo founders win on x while doing way less of the busywork. so i broke down exactly how they pull it off.

it isn't discipline. they don't grind demo videos, og images, reels, a newsletter, a blog, and a posting schedule by hand. they build one system that makes all of it, and aim it at one channel.

here's how to build each piece:

1. build a loop, not a checklist.

four stages, four folders: ideas, draft, publish, learn.
- ideas: a running file the system keeps filling from what's already working in your niche
- voice: reverse-engineer your own 10 best posts into a traits file. sentence length, how you open, what you never do
- draft: one prompt that loads the voice file plus a single idea
- learn: log what got bookmarked, feed that back into which ideas get picked next

every surface (x, blog, newsletter) is just a different publish target hanging off the same drafted piece. build the loop once, not the chores forever.

2. chain specialists. stop one-shotting it.

five prompt files, one job each:
- strategist: topic + audience in, angle + hook + brief out
- researcher: brief in, sources + facts + 3 contrarian points out
- writer: brief + research in, full draft out
- editor: cuts 30%, sharpens the opening, rewrites the close
- publisher: formats for the target platform

output of one becomes input to the next. it beats a single chat for a concrete reason: an editor in a fresh window will actually cut what a writer "worked hard on." same window, it won't, because it watched the writer struggle. you touch it twice. two paragraphs in, approve at the end.

3. build the faceless video factory, then give it a brain.

the pipeline is script, voice, assembly, post, measure.
- claude writes the script. pick the niche by rpm and competition gap, not by what you personally like
- elevenlabs voices it
- capcut or any auto-editor assembles the clips or the slideshow
- a scheduler api drops it in as a draft so you can add trending audio before it publishes

the step everyone skips is the one that pays. wire the agent to read the funnel: views, then installs, then subscribers. it logs every hook's result and rewrites its own rules over time. an agent that just posts is noise. an agent that reads the funnel is distribution.

4. aim the whole machine at one channel: the one where your product is the audience.

before you automate anything, answer one question. where does my buyer already sit, and is my product about that place?

build a tool for x creators, sell it on x. the audience is pre-qualified, so even a post with 8 likes brings real leads.

the mistake is spreading across five platforms on day one and ending up with five weak channels. point everything at the single tightest product-to-audience fit. saturate it. expand only after it's working.

5. start the blog on day one, and write for your competitors' tools too.

this is the channel that compounds while you sleep.
- target the exact queries people type when they already have the problem. "where are X stored", "how to install Y"
- one article per query, and make every heading a question
- put a 40 to 60 word answer block at the very top. that block is what chatgpt and perplexity pull and cite
- add schema markup on every page (article, faq, howto)
- write guides for adjacent and competitor tools you don't even make. those queries have almost no competition

start before the product is finished. seo's clock starts at article one, so the earlier you begin the bigger the head start.

one catch. the system makes the content. it does not make the replies.

the fastest growth i found still came down to someone treating replies like a full-time job. short sessions through the day, real conversations, not broadcasts. automate the machine. you're still the one who talks to people.

so: which one channel are you going all in on, and what's the first surface you automate to feed it? specific moves only.

I found a faceless YouTube channel making $39,500/month from AdSense alone.

It's called Bright Side. Documentary-style educational videos. No host. No crew. All AI-generated.

So I asked: can I replicate that entire channel in 20 minutes using AI?

I did. And it took just two prompts.

Here's the exact playbook:

First, I connected Claude (Anthropic's latest model) to Higgsfield AI's MCP tool. Took 2 minutes — just copy a URL and paste it into Claude's settings.

Then I sent one prompt: "Analyze this channel's scripts and hooks, then write a script for a similar video." I included the channel link.

Claude studied their top videos, identified the pattern, chose a topic, and wrote a full script.

Second prompt: "Generate a 5-minute 1080p video for a faceless YouTube channel using Seedance 2.0."

Claude auto-split the script into scenes, generated visuals, voiceover, and music — all consistent in style. Took 10 minutes.

Here's a sample from the output:

"Look at that mountain. In a few hours, it will wipe out an entire city. 2,000 years later, we're still digging out those who didn't run. This is Pompeii. Today is your last day here."

Then Claude auto-generated a title, description, tags, and 3 thumbnail options for A/B testing. I just uploaded the video file, pasted the text, and scheduled it.

I asked it to make two more videos on different topics. It researched new themes and produced completely different scripts and visuals.

After 3 days, the new channel had views and subs. Not $39,500 yet — but the process works.

Now, the revenue claim: the creator reportedly says Bright Side earns $39,500/month. I can't verify that. But YouTube education RPM is $5-15 per 1,000 views. Millions of views make those numbers plausible.

Caveat: YouTube requires 1,000 subs and 4,000 watch hours for monetization. AI content passes review if it's original, deep, and well-edited. Low-effort junk gets demonetized fast.

This workflow cuts the barrier to entry. No editing skills. No scriptwriting. No face. Even prompt engineering is optional — Claude writes its own prompts.

But low barrier means fast competition. The winners will be those who understand audience needs and deliver real value. AI is an accelerator, not a money printer.

Try Higgsfield MCP + Claude if you're curious about AI video. But treat it as a skill to learn, not a shortcut to wealth.

→ A loop that scopes every client build before the call so I walk in ready
